headline: High-risk shared-write and data-exposure pathways exist: Replit Agent’s writable Repl workspace plus broad egress can conflict with oh-my-openagent’s injected MCP/hooks and provider-auth handling.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A can use runtime-injected MCPs and hooks, and B can read/write the Repl workspace; that creates a plausible instruction-injection bridge if A’s outputs are placed into files B later parses. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than observed.
conditions: IF agent_a writes instructions into files that agent_b later reads as prompts or config, injection is possible.
IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or synced files, the bridge becomes active.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories or repos.
Disable file-based prompt ingestion for either agent.
Add a provenance marker to any file passed between agents.
Review any shared MCP or hook outputs before reuse.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches provider authentication data and session history, while B touches secrets and deployment configuration and has broad network egress. If they share a workspace or credentials, either agent could expose sensitive material through its outbound calls. The exact sharing mechanism is not documented, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share files containing auth data or secrets, leakage is possible.
IF either agent is given the other’s workspace contents, outbound exfiltration becomes plausible.
mitigations: Keep secrets in separate stores per agent.
Remove auth files from any shared directory.
Block outbound network access during cross-agent handoff.
Rotate any credentials that were present in shared workspaces.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write to filesystem-like workspaces, and B can modify git state while A can spawn subprocesses and operate with full-permissions mode. In a shared repo or Repl, concurrent writes can overwrite each other or corrupt state; the profiles do not show locking, so the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or workspace, write conflicts can occur.
IF git state is modified without external locking, concurrent edits can corrupt history or branches.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working tree.
Serialize git operations through one operator.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
Add a lock file before any write or commit step.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can produce code-navigation and task outputs through MCP/hooks, and B is a coding agent that can act on workspace contents and modify git state. That makes A’s output a plausible upstream input for B, but B is not documented as blindly trusting A, so this is a medium cascade risk rather than high.
conditions: IF agent_a’s generated instructions are copied into agent_b’s prompt or files, B may act on them.
IF B is configured to auto-commit or auto-deploy A-derived changes, errors can cascade.
mitigations: Require human review before B acts on A output.
Use a diff-only handoff format.
Add a verification step for any A-generated facts or code.
Disable auto-commit and auto-deploy paths.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles provider authentication data and session history, while B handles secrets and deployment configuration in a Replit-managed cloud workspace. That creates a plausible retention and residency mismatch if the same regulated data is moved between them, but no specific jurisdictional conflict is documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is copied from agent_a into agent_b’s Repl workspace, retention and residency controls may diverge.
IF either agent logs secrets or auth prompts longer than intended, compliance exposure increases.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces.
Confirm retention settings for both environments.
Redact secrets before transfer between agents.
Document which agent is allowed to store which data class.
